sections.title: One number, several names

passages.title: A denominator chooses the unit
passages.text:
An integer names a whole-number position.

A rational number is a quotient p/q of integers with q ≠ 0. We may put any negative sign in p and choose q > 0. To read 3/4, first divide one whole into four equal parts, then take three parts.

The numerator counts selected parts; the denominator determines their size. If each part is halved, we now have six selected eighths. The amount has not changed: both names point to the same number.

Every integer is rational too, since m = m/1.

steps.text: Show one whole cut into two equal pieces; select one.
Cut both halves in half. The selected half now contains two of the four pieces.

check.explanation: The pieces are smaller, but twice as many are selected. The amount stays one half.

simplerHelp.connection: The numerator and denominator describe a representation; the fixed amount is the number.

sections.title: Division explains a repeating name

passages.title: A repeated remainder repeats the future
passages.text:
A decimal digit can be constructed rather than guessed.

For 1/6, divide 10 by 6: the next digit is 1 and the remainder is 4. Multiply that remainder by 10; 40 = 6·6 + 4 gives the next digit 6 and returns the same remainder. The identical calculation will now repeat.

More generally, a denominator q allows only q possible nonnegative remainders. Either remainder 0 ends the decimal, or a nonzero remainder repeats and forces a repeating block. A recurring decimal can therefore be an exact rational representation.

sections.title: Exact values need not have finite names

passages.title: A real number can be located by narrowing bounds
passages.text:
A rational number has an integer-ratio name; an irrational real number does not.

A decimal that does not terminate is not automatically irrational: 1/3 is a counterexample. The positive square root of 2 is irrational, but rational bounds locate it: 1.4² < 2 < 1.5² and 1.41² < 2 < 1.42². The squares justify the bounds because squaring is increasing for nonnegative numbers.

Refining such bounds distinguishes the exact number from any finite drawing or decimal approximation. The book chooses decimal representations without an infinite tail of 9s to avoid duplicate names; as an equality of real values, 0.999… = 1 remains true.

sections.title: An exponent counts factors

passages.title: Each factor multiplies the whole current amount
passages.text:
For a positive integer n, bⁿ means n copies of b multiplied together.

In 3⁴ the base is 3, the exponent is 4, and the value is 81. Start with one unit and replace every unit by three units at each step: 1, 3, 9, 27, 81. The exponent counts how many factors have been used, not how many units exist at the end.

Thus 3⁴, 4·3, and 4³ are different expressions. A picture may group units to stay readable, but the labeled multiplicity must account for every unit.

sections.title: Read the laws from the factor structure

passages.title: Multiplying powers joins their factor lists
passages.text:
Suppose m and n are positive integers and the base is the same in both powers.

The first product has m factors b and the second has n factors b. Multiplying the products joins the two lists, so there are m+n factors altogether. For instance, 2³·2² joins three twos and two twos to make 2⁵.

Nothing in this argument permits adding the exponents of different bases: the joined list would no longer consist of one repeated factor.

The expression (bᵐ)ⁿ uses bᵐ as a factor n times.

title: Zero, negative, and rational powers

sections.title: Extend powers without breaking the pattern

passages.title: Moving backward divides by the base
passages.text:
We now require b > 0.

Moving from exponent k to k+1 multiplies by b, so moving backward must divide by b. For base 2, the sequence 2² = 4, 2¹ = 2 continues to 2⁰ = 1, then 2⁻¹ = 1/2 and 2⁻² = 1/4. These choices preserve the same-base exponent law.

In particular bⁿb⁻ⁿ = b⁰ = 1, so b⁻ⁿ = 1/bⁿ. A negative exponent asks for a reciprocal; it does not make the value negative. Zero has no reciprocal, and 0⁰ is outside this lesson’s chosen positive-base domain.

sections.title: Split an exponent into equal parts

passages.title: A fractional exponent names a positive root
passages.text:
If an exponent step of one is split into q equal steps, applying all q steps must multiply by b.

We therefore define b^(1/q) as the unique positive qth root of b: the positive value v satisfying v^q = b. For b = 16 and q = 2, that value is 4, because 4² = 16. Although the equation z² = 16 has the two real solutions 4 and −4, the symbol √16 and the power 16^(1/2) designate only the positive root.

Restricting the base to positive values makes these definitions consistent throughout this lesson.

sections.title: Root, power, reciprocal are separate operations

passages.title: Root, power, reciprocal are separate operations
passages.text:
For a rational exponent p/q, with integer p and positive integer q, define b^(p/q) = (b^(1/q))^p.

First find the positive qth root, then raise it to the integer power p. A negative p introduces the reciprocal after the positive power. For 16^(−3/2), the positive square root is 4, the third power is 64, and the reciprocal is 1/64.

Reading those operations separately prevents a negative exponent from being confused with a negative base or with a negative root.

sections.title: The value must not depend on the fraction’s spelling

passages.title: The value must not depend on the fraction’s spelling
passages.text:
The exponents 1/2 and 2/4 are the same rational number, so a sound definition must assign the same power.

For 16, taking its fourth root gives 2 and then squaring gives 4, just as taking its square root does. More generally, if v is the positive qth root of b, then v^p is also the unique positive solution of w^q = b^p. Replacing p/q by ap/(aq), for a positive integer a, gives the same positive value: its aqth power is b^(ap).

This consistency is why the exponent denotes a number, rather than a particular pair of written integers.

title: Logarithms as inverses

source.book: Donald E. Knuth, The Art of Computer Programming, Volume 1, third edition

sections.title: Before inverting, fill the gaps between powers

passages.title: Rational bounds define a real exponent
passages.text:
Integer and rational exponents do not yet cover every real exponent.

For b > 1, choose rational lower and upper bounds ℓ < x < u. Rational powers increase with their exponents, so b^ℓ < b^x < b^u is the behavior we require. As decimal bounds for x tighten, the two power bounds approach the same positive limit; that common value defines b^x.

The book justifies that the gap can be made arbitrarily small. For 0 < b < 1, define b^x = (1/b)^(−x); this gives decreasing powers. A few visible brackets illustrate the construction, while the shrinking-gap argument, not a finite animation, establishes a unique value.

sections.title: Recover the exponent from a positive value

passages.title: A logarithm asks which exponent reaches the target
passages.text:
Fix b > 0 with b ≠ 1.

For every positive y, there is exactly one real exponent x with b^x = y. We call that exponent log_b y. For b > 1 the power function is strictly increasing; for 0 < b < 1 it is strictly decreasing.

Together with continuity and the positive range, this ensures existence and uniqueness. Base 1 is excluded because 1^x is always 1, so it cannot give a unique inverse. The notation lg y means log₂ y.

A log is an exponent, not the positive value that the exponent produces.

passages.title: A logarithm need not be a whole-number count
passages.text:
The inverse definition covers fractional and irrational exponents.

Since 4^(1/2) = 2, log₄2 = 1/2 exactly. For lg 3, no integer exponent works: 2¹ < 3 < 2² implies 1 < lg 3 < 2. We can improve the bracket without guessing decimal digits.

Because 2^(3/2) = √8 < 3 and 2^(7/4) > 3, we obtain 3/2 < lg 3 < 7/4. The latter comparison follows by raising positive quantities to the fourth power: 2⁷ = 128 > 3⁴ = 81. Logs between integer ticks are genuine exponents, not partial counts of completed integer multiplications.

For base 1/2, increasing the exponent shrinks the value: (1/2)⁰ = 1, (1/2)¹ = 1/2, and (1/2)² = 1/4.

sections.title: Logarithms turn multiplication into addition

passages.title: Join multiplication paths and add exponent distances
passages.text:
Keep one valid base b fixed, and let u and v be positive.

Write u = bˣ and v = bʸ, so x = log_b u and y = log_b v. Multiplication gives uv = bˣbʸ = b^(x+y). Taking the logarithm recovers exponent x+y.

For example, multiplying 8 by 4 follows three doublings and then two more, reaching 32 after five doublings. The exponent axis measures additive exponent distance; the value axis measures the corresponding positive numbers. passages.title: Undo a path, or scale its exponent distance
passages.text:
Division reverses a multiplication path.

If u = bˣ and v = bʸ, then u/v = b^(x−y), so log_b(u/v) = log_b u − log_b v. Likewise uʳ = (bˣ)ʳ = b^(rx), giving log_b(uʳ) = r log_b u for real r and positive u. In the integer example lg(32/4), retrace two of five exponent steps to end at 3.

In lg(4³), repeat the two-step exponent distance three times to reach 6. The laws come from exponent identities, not from the shapes or lengths of positive-value bars.

sections.title: Change the exponent unit without changing the target

passages.title: Change the exponent unit without changing the target
passages.text:
Let z = log_b x, so x = bᶻ.

Taking logarithms in another valid base c gives log_c x = z log_c b. Since b ≠ 1, the factor log_c b is nonzero, so division yields log_b x = log_c x / log_c b. For target 64, six doublings and two multiplications by 8 reach the same value.

One base-8 step is three base-2 steps, so divide the six binary steps by three: log₈64 = lg 64 / lg 8 = 2. This rescaling works for real exponents too; integer step drawings are an illustration of the algebra, not its only domain.

sections.title: Addition inside a logarithm has no analogous rule

passages.title: Addition inside a logarithm has no analogous rule
passages.text:
The product rule does not permit log_b(u+v) = log_b u + log_b v.

Let x be an exact value and x̂ its recorded approximation.

sections.title: An error bound is not the error itself

passages.title: An error bound is not the error itself
passages.text:
Rounding a real value x to the nearest multiple of 10^(−d) produces x̂ with |x̂−x| ≤ 1/(2·10ᵈ), regardless of which tie-breaking rule chooses an endpoint.

If the same rounded value is added q times, with q a nonnegative integer, then qx̂−qx = q(x̂−x), so its absolute error is at most q/(2·10ᵈ). For three thirds rounded to two decimal places, the bound is 3/200 = 0.015, while the actual absolute error is 0.01. A guarantee can be larger than the realized error.

This bound concerns nearest rounding and repeated addition, not arbitrary measurement errors or nonlinear recurrences.

sections.title: Changing when you round can change the result

passages.title: Changing when you round can change the result
passages.text:
Compare two routes for three copies of 1/3.

Rounding each copy first gives 0.33+0.33+0.33 = 0.99. Adding exactly first gives 1, which rounded to two decimal places is 1.00. Thus rounding does not commute with addition.

Keeping exact fractions longer avoids these particular early-rounding errors, although real computations may have precision and cost constraints. Two decimal places means a grid with spacing 0.01. Two significant figures means two meaningful leading digits, so its spacing depends on magnitude: 123.4 to two significant figures is 120, whereas to two decimal places it is 123.40.

sections.title: A finite rearrangement needs a one-to-one matching

passages.title: A finite rearrangement needs a one-to-one matching
passages.text:
Reversing a finite list changes its order, not its terms.

For indices k=0,1,2,3, set j=3−k. The inverse relation is k=3−j, so Σ from k=0 to 3 of a_k equals Σ from j=0 to 3 of a_(3−j). The new order reads a₃,a₂,a₁,a₀.

Every original card appears exactly once, which establishes preservation independently of an accidental equality of totals. A relabeling that duplicates one card or skips another is not a bijection. These finite rearrangements do not authorize arbitrary rearrangement of an infinite series.

demonstration.title: A finite rearrangement needs a one-to-one matching

model.domain: finite four-term sum; bijection j=3−k

states.caption: Four distinct term cards have values 2, 5, 1, 4.
Attach new labels j=3−k to the same cards.
Arrange by increasing j; each old card occurs once, in reverse order.

transitions.explanation: Connect every original index to exactly one new index.
Move entire cards; retain their original identities and values, and sort only by the new labels.

check.prompt: What proves this is a valid finite reindexing?
choices: The totals happen to look equal
Every original term has exactly one new position
check.explanation: A bijection prevents missing or repeated terms. Equal numeric totals alone could conceal substitutions.

simplerHelp.intro: Reverse just three cards with values 2, 5, 1.

steps.text: Give each card a distinct identity, even if two values might later coincide.
Move the last to first, keep the middle, move first to last.
The values become 1,5,2, with the same three contributions.

check.prompt: If one card is copied twice and another omitted, is that a reindexing?
choices: Yes if the total coincidentally matches
Yes if the labels still look consecutive
check.explanation: A valid relabeling matches original terms one-to-one, not merely totals.

simplerHelp.connection: Finite rearrangement preserves the multiset of term occurrences, including multiplicity.

title: Arithmetic sums by pairing

source.book: Donald E. Knuth, The Art of Computer Programming, Volume 1, third edition

provenance: Original explanation, worked examples, questions, and visual models after the cited concepts. The textbook is unchanged; no textbook prose, PDF, or page image is included.

sections.title: Count the gaps before finding the endpoint

passages.title: n terms contain n−1 steps of the common difference
passages.text:
An arithmetic progression starts at a and adds a fixed difference d each time.

With n ≥ 1 terms and zero-based indices, term k is a+kd for k=0,…,n−1. The last term is therefore a+(n−1)d. For the four terms 2,5,8,11, there are three gaps of size 3, not four.

The number of terms and the number of gaps play different roles: n counts contributions to the sum, while n−1 counts changes needed to reach the last contribution.

demonstration.title: n terms contain n−1 steps of the common difference

model.domain: n positive integer; a,d real

states.caption: One term 2 has been placed, using zero gaps.
Add difference 3 once to get the second term 5.
Four terms use only three additions of 3 to reach the endpoint 11.

transitions.explanation: Draw one connecting gap arrow labeled +3; increase term and gap counters separately.
Append 8 and then 11 with separate +3 arrows; retain all four term identities.

check.prompt: What is the fifth term starting from 2 with difference 3?
check.explanation: The fifth term uses four gaps: 2+4·3=14. Multiplying the difference by five would go one term too far.

simplerHelp.intro: Lay down only three cards: 2, 5, 8.

steps.text: The first card needs no step from the starting value.
Two arrows labeled +3 connect three cards.
The third term is 2+2·3, so three terms use n−1=2 gaps.

check.prompt: How many gaps are there between six consecutive terms?
check.explanation: Each new term after the first adds one gap.

simplerHelp.connection: n counts cards; n−1 counts the transitions between them.

sections.title: Reverse a second copy so every column has the same sum

passages.title: Reverse a second copy so every column has the same sum
passages.text:
Write the n terms in one row, then make a second complete copy and reverse its order.

Pair corresponding columns. The first column contains a and a+(n−1)d; in every next column the upper term increases by d while the lower decreases by d. Each column therefore has the same sum 2a+(n−1)d.

There are n columns, and the two rows together contain two copies of the original total S. Hence 2S = n(2a+(n−1)d), and dividing by 2 gives the arithmetic-sum formula. Odd n causes no exception: the middle term appears once in each full copy.

demonstration.title: Reverse a second copy so every column has the same sum

model.domain: n positive integer; a,d real; demonstrated a=2,d=3,n=3

states.caption: The original row 2, 5, 8 has total S.
Create a second complete row with new copy identities.
Reverse only the copied row: 8, 5, 2 now align below 2, 5, 8.
Combine each upper/lower pair into a column of 10. The middle 5 is used twice because there are two rows.
Half the double total is the original sum, 15.

transitions.explanation: Create visibly distinct copies; the represented sum doubles at this step.
Move copied cards to reversed positions without changing any value.
Each column’s two card values combine to 10; retain source colors in the merged column.
Explicitly account for two copies before returning to one; do not silently discard a row.

check.prompt: Why is the middle value 5 counted twice in the three-term example?
choices: We deliberately made two complete copies
Odd-length sums need an extra term
The middle value does not belong to S
check.explanation: The argument computes 2S first. Each original term, including the middle one, appears once in each copy.

simplerHelp.intro: Pair 2,5,8 with the reversed copy 8,5,2.

steps.text: Keep both rows visible.
The three columns each total 10.
Three tens give 30 for two copies; one copy is 15.

check.prompt: What is 1+4+7 using the same pairing?
check.explanation: The reversed copy is 7,4,1. Three columns total 8 each, so 2S=24 and S=12.

simplerHelp.connection: The formula counts equal pair totals, then compensates for the duplicated list.

sections.title: Pairing is algebra, so decreasing and signed terms still work

passages.title: Pairing is algebra, so decreasing and signed terms still work
passages.text:
The pairing identity does not require d or the terms to be positive.

For 5,2,−1, the common difference is −3. Pair this row with −1,2,5: every column sums to 4, so 2S=12 and S=6. Negative entries must be shown as signed values or directed changes, not negative physical lengths.

A one-term list also works: n=1 gives S=a because its two copies total 2a. For n=0 we use the empty-sum convention S=0; there is no last term to point to, although the algebraic formula n(2a+(n−1)d)/2 still evaluates to zero.

demonstration.title: Pairing is algebra, so decreasing and signed terms still work

model.domain: real a,d; n nonnegative integer; zero treated as an empty list

states.caption: The original terms are +5, +2, and −1.
The reversed copy has −1, +2, +5; signs remain attached to cards.
Each signed pair gives +4; the negative units cancel one positive unit in the outer columns.
Dividing 12 by 2 returns the signed sum 6.

transitions.explanation: Preserve plus and minus signs explicitly while making the reversed copy.
Use signed tokens or a zero-baseline number line; never encode a negative value as unsigned area.
Return from two signed copies to one.

check.prompt: Does the arithmetic-sum formula require d>0?
choices: Yes; otherwise there are negative lengths
No; it also works for decreasing sequences
check.explanation: The derivation pairs algebraic values. The example d=−3 gives valid equal column sums; geometry must respect signs.

simplerHelp.intro: Use just 3 and −1.

steps.text: Three positive units and one negative unit leave 2.
The reversed copy is −1,3; each column gives 2.
The two columns total 4 for two copies, so one copy totals 2.

check.prompt: What is the sum of an arithmetic list with zero terms?
check.explanation: An empty sum selects no terms and has value zero; no actual last term exists.

simplerHelp.connection: Signs change values, and emptiness changes the index set, but the finite algebra remains consistent.

title: Geometric sums by signed cancellation

source.book: Donald E. Knuth, The Art of Computer Programming, Volume 1, third edition

provenance: Original explanation, worked examples, questions, and visual models after the cited concepts. The textbook is unchanged; no textbook prose, PDF, or page image is included.
scope: Original n-term convention with exponents 0 through n−1, differing from the source’s endpoint convention. Explicit signed cancellation, r=1, n=0, n=1, and finite-versus-infinite distinction.

sections.title: Multiplying a geometric sum shifts its powers

passages.title: Copy the sum, then multiply every term by the ratio
passages.text:
For a nonnegative integer n, let Sₙ contain the n terms 1,r,…,r^(n−1).

Each term is obtained by multiplying its predecessor by the common ratio r. Multiplying the whole sum by r multiplies every term, giving r,r²,…,rⁿ. The two rows overlap in powers r through r^(n−1), but they have different endpoints.

Keep the original row while making the multiplied copy: cancellation will compare two expressions, not erase terms during multiplication. The worked example uses r=2,n=4, so S₄=1+2+4+8 and 2S₄=2+4+8+16.

demonstration.title: Copy the sum, then multiply every term by the ratio

model.domain: finite geometric list; main example r=2,n=4

states.caption: Four original powers occupy exponents 0 through 3.
Duplicate the entire original sum before changing the copy.
Each copied card is multiplied by 2 and moves to exponent k+1; the original is unchanged.

transitions.explanation: The new row begins as a copy; each source and copy has its own stable identity.
Double each copied value, increase its exponent by one, then align cards by exponent rather than original position.

check.prompt: After multiplying 1+2+4+8 by 2, which term appears at the new right endpoint?
check.explanation: Every term is multiplied by 2. The last original term 8 becomes 16, corresponding to exponent 4.

simplerHelp.intro: Start with 1+2+4.

steps.text: Make a second row 1,2,4.
Double each copied card to get 2,4,8.
Align equal powers: 2 over 2 and 4 over 4. The endpoints are 1 and 8.

check.prompt: Which power lies only in the multiplied row?
check.explanation: Multiplication shifts exponents up by one, so the new highest power has no original-row partner.

simplerHelp.connection: A shifted power list creates the overlap needed for the next subtraction.

sections.title: Subtract the original row and cancel opposite-signed equals

passages.title: Subtract the original row and cancel opposite-signed equals
passages.text:
For n ≥ 1, subtract Sₙ from rSₙ.

Write subtraction on every original term: the lower row contributes −1,−r,…,−r^(n−1). Each overlapping power now appears once with a plus sign and once with a minus sign, so those paired occurrences sum to zero. The survivors are +rⁿ from the multiplied row and −1 from the original row.

Thus rSₙ−Sₙ = rⁿ−1, or (r−1)Sₙ = rⁿ−1. When r ≠ 1, divide by the nonzero factor r−1. Cancellation is removal of opposite-signed equal terms, not arbitrary deletion of visually similar cards.

demonstration.title: Subtract the original row and cancel opposite-signed equals

model.domain: n≥1; real r; division only when r≠1

states.caption: The multiplied row and original row are aligned by exponent.
Mark the whole lower row as subtracted; every lower sign becomes negative.
The +2 and −2 pair have visibly canceled to zero.
The +4/−4 and +8/−8 pairs cancel too. Only +16 and −1 remain.
The nonzero factor is 2−1=1; divide to obtain S₄=15.

transitions.explanation: A visible minus bracket covers the whole row before each term gets its negative sign.
Bring +2 and −2 together, show their sum 0, then fade their card bodies; leave a zero trace.
Cancel +4 with −4 and +8 with −8 sequentially. Keep endpoints visible throughout.
Check r−1 is nonzero before dividing; relate one remaining S to the endpoint difference.

check.prompt: Which terms survive rSₙ−Sₙ after matching interior powers?
check.explanation: The largest power comes from the positive multiplied row; the constant 1 comes from the subtracted original row and therefore has a minus sign.

steps.text: Write the subtraction as +2+4+8−1−2−4.
Pair +2 with −2 and +4 with −4; make each pair disappear only after showing zero.
The survivors are +8−1=7. Since 2S−S=S, the original sum is 7.

check.prompt: In (3+9+27)−(1+3+9), which terms survive?
check.explanation: The shared +3/−3 and +9/−9 cancel, leaving the signed endpoints.

simplerHelp.connection: The negative sign belongs to every term of the subtracted row; matched pairs cancel because their signed sum is zero.

sections.title: At ratio one, count terms instead of dividing by zero

passages.title: At ratio one, count terms instead of dividing by zero
passages.text:
When r=1, every term of Sₙ equals 1, so Sₙ=n.

The cancellation identity becomes 0·Sₙ=0, which is true but tells us nothing about Sₙ. Substituting r=1 into (rⁿ−1)/(r−1) gives 0/0, not n and not zero. The valid computation is to count the n unit terms.

Identical numerical values still have separate occurrences: three cards equal to 1 are three contributions. Cancellation must respect those multiplicities and signs.

demonstration.title: At ratio one, count terms instead of dividing by zero

model.domain: r=1; integer n≥0; demonstration n=3

states.caption: Three distinct unit cards contribute 1+1+1.
Multiplying by ratio 1 changes nothing; subtracting the same sum gives 0=0.
Return to the original terms and count all three unit occurrences.

transitions.explanation: Show the r−1 test and block division; do not evaluate 0/0 as a number.
Count the three original occurrences exactly once each.

check.prompt: What is S₅ when r=1?
check.explanation: The original finite sum is five ones and is defined. Only the quotient formula is unavailable at r=1.

simplerHelp.intro: Take only two unit cards.

steps.text: Two separate cards each contribute 1.
Their sum is 2.
The expression (1²−1)/(1−1) cannot compute that value because its denominator is zero.

check.prompt: Does a failed quotient formula mean the original sum is undefined?
check.explanation: The finite sum of unit terms remains well-defined; a derivation that divides by zero is invalid.

simplerHelp.connection: Domain restrictions belong to a formula, and must be checked before using it.

sections.title: Check empty and one-term sums before thinking about limits

passages.title: Check empty and one-term sums before thinking about limits
passages.text:
With n=0, the finite index set is empty, so S₀=0.

For r≠1, the quotient agrees: (r⁰−1)/(r−1)=0. With n=1, there is exactly the constant term 1, so S₁=1, and (r−1)/(r−1)=1 when r≠1. These are checks of the derived formula, not a proof of all n.

A finite geometric sum is defined even for ratios larger than one; no convergence condition is needed. If we later let n grow without bound, a different question arises. For |r|<1, rⁿ tends to zero and the finite identity yields the infinite sum 1/(1−r); for the displayed ratio 2, the finite sums instead grow without bound.

demonstration.title: Check empty and one-term sums before thinking about limits

model.domain: n≥0; real r; the initial constant term is 1, also when r=0
model.notationNote: At r=0, view the finite sum as the polynomial 1+r+…; its constant term is 1. This is a polynomial convention, not a general claim about every context involving 0⁰.

states.caption: At n=0 there are no term cards. The finite sum is zero.
At n=1 a single constant term 1 appears.
At n=2 with ratio 2, append exactly one next term, 2.

transitions.explanation: Start with no cards, then add the constant term exactly once.
Multiply the preceding term by r=2; increase the term count by one.

check.prompt: Does ratio 2 make the four-term sum 1+2+4+8 invalid?
choices: No; it is the finite sum 15
check.explanation: The convergence condition belongs to the infinite series. Every displayed finite sum has only finitely many additions.

simplerHelp.intro: Compare an empty tray with a tray containing one card labeled 1.

steps.text: No cards give total 0.
One constant card gives total 1, regardless of the ratio used for later terms.
n counts terms; it is not the largest exponent, which is n−1 for a nonempty list.

check.prompt: What is the highest exponent in a nonempty four-term geometric sum starting at 1?
check.explanation: The exponents are 0,1,2,3. There are four terms and three multiplicative gaps.

simplerHelp.connection: Boundary checks confirm the meaning of n and prevent an off-by-one error in the endpoint rⁿ.
